summary:
Earth Trend Detective is a research prototype that helps users investigate regional climate changes using NASA GISTEMP temperature data and GPCP precipitation observations. We developed a Python analysis core and an interactive web interface with regional time series, trend estimates, data-quality reports, machine-learning screening results and downloadable evidence.

The system checks source integrity, missing observations, seasonal patterns and spatial coverage before producing regional results. A separate scenario viewer compares CMIP6 temperature projections under two emissions pathways for a demonstration location.

Our tool addresses the challenge by connecting Earth observation data with visual explanations of what is changing, where changes occur and how large they are. It also makes uncertainty visible: statistical results remain exploratory where calibration has failed, and ML flags identify candidates for investigation.

This matters because misleading climate conclusions can arise from incomplete data or inappropriate analysis. Traceable results help students, researchers and scientifically interested users explore environmental change with a clearer understanding of the evidence and its limits.
details:
Earth Trend Detective is a research platform for exploring changes in Earth's climate using global temperature and precipitation data. It combines NASA GISTEMP and GPCP observations with regional time series, quality reports and interactive visualizations.

Its Python core verifies source files, preserves units and reference periods, checks missing observations and seasonal variation, and computes area-weighted regional aggregates. Users can examine trend estimates and a machine-learning detector trained on historical data and evaluated on a separate period. MUSE integration checks the scope and references of scientific artifacts, making results traceable to their inputs.

The web interface presents reproducible regional examples, quality evidence, ML screening flags and downloadable results. A separate CMIP6 module compares temperature changes under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 for one grid cell near Berlin, using World Bank climate projections. It displays model spread without treating it as a probability.

The project prioritizes reproducibility and honest uncertainty. Statistical calibration failures remain visible, and ML flags are exploratory signals rather than confirmed discoveries. It helps students, researchers and scientifically interested users investigate what is changing, where, and by how much.
